fractionally to the east of the main solstitial axis
Immediately outside the north-east entrance is the Heel Stone, a huge unshaped sarsen boulder.

slaughter_stone_position.value: in the north-east entrance, midway between the circle and the Heel Stone, just east of the axis

cites.quote: The Slaughter Stone lies prone, midway between the central monument and the Heel Stone just east of the primary solstitial axis.

value.direction: north-east from the entrance along the solstice axis (azimuth ~49.6 deg near the monument)
value.width_m: about 12 between the banks (EH); about 20 including banks and ditches (EH audio); Lockyer about 50 feet

avenue.note: Width figures disagree (12 m corridor vs 20 m vs ~15 m); probably measured to different edges.

cites.quote: Today it can be seen in part as low parallel banks enclosing a corridor about 12 metres wide.
They form a corridor running towards Stonehenge about 20
receiving into itself the banks forming the avenue before mentioned, which is about 50 feet across
it measures nearly 3 kilometres, and connects Stonehenge with the River Avon
Along some of its length, the avenue is aligned with the sunrise of the summer solstice

bank_and_ditch.value: circular ditch with an internal bank and a smaller external bank, about 100-110 m across, main entrance north-east, smaller one south

cites.quote: Today the ditch and inner bank are visible as low earthworks in the grass, but the outer bank has largely been ploughed away.
with a large entrance to the north east and a smaller one to the south

bluestone_settings.value: a circle between the sarsen circle and the trilithons, and an inner horseshoe (formerly an oval) inside the trilithons, open to the north-east

cites.quote: About 200 or 300 years later the central bluestones were rearranged to form a circle and inner oval (which was again later altered to form a horseshoe).
the northeastern section of the Phase 3 IV bluestone circle was removed, creating a horseshoe-shaped setting (the Bluestone Horseshoe) which mirrored the shape of the central sarsen Trilithons

construction_dates.value: sarsens c. 2620-2480 BC (all three sarsen structures, Stage 2); bluestones in their present positions c. 2400-2200 BC

cites.quote: were set up during the period 2620–2480 BC
Radiocarbon dating suggests that the bluestones were given their current positions between 2400 and 2200 BC

missing_debate.claim: The present monument is incomplete; it has been suggested that the sarsen circle was only ever finished on the north-eastern side.

cites.quote: Yet Stonehenge in its present form is incomplete—some of the expected stones are missing—and it has sometimes been suggested that it was never complete

missing_debate.claim: In the dry summer of 2013 parchmarks appeared in the south-west where missing uprights should stand (around 16-20), evidence of stoneholes.

cites.quote: an exceptionally dry summer in 2013 revealed patches of parched grass which may correspond to the location of missing sarsens
a series of parch marks appeared in the circuit exactly where some of the missing uprights should be

missing_debate.claim: Darvill (2022): sockets for some missing uprights are known by excavation, the rest from the parchmarks; jointing shows a complete circuit was intended; the missing uprights and lintels were robbed in antiquity.

cites.quote: As such, it must be concluded that the missing sarsen uprights and lintels were robbed in antiquity.
provide evidence of an intention to form a compete circuit

missing_debate.claim: Field et al. (2015): the evidence is not conclusive; the circle may have been built as a facade with other parts added and an entrance in the south. They also suggest a lintelled bluestone trilithon formed an entrance in the north-east.

cites.quote: This work has added detail that allows discussion on the question of whether the sarsen circle was a completed structure, although it is by no means conclusive in this respect.
it is suggested that it was built as a façade, with other parts of the circuit added and with an entrance in the south
The probability that a lintelled bluestone trilithon formed an entrance in the north-east is signposted.

missing_debate.claim: English Heritage remains cautious ('if it was ever completed'); the earlier view that the circle was never completed (Ashbee 1998) is cited by Darvill.

cites.quote: if it was ever completed, there would have been an unbroken ring of stone
Although the missing stones have sometimes been suggested to indicate that the Sarsen Circle was never completed (e.g. Ashbee Reference Ashbee1998)

missing_debate.claim: A complete design needs 75 sarsens in the circle and horseshoe (60 + 15); 52 sarsens survive on site in all.

cites.quote: A total of 75 stones would have been needed to complete the circle (60 stones) and the trilithon horseshoe (15 stones).
50 of the 52 sarsens at the monument share a consistent chemistry

missing_debate.claim: All 15 trilithon stones survive on site (none robbed); bluestones: about 80 assumed originally, 43 survive.

cites.quote: All stones survive on site, although some have fallen.
only 43 remain

missing_debate.claim: The Heel Stone had a companion (S97) whose hole was found in 1979; the Slaughter Stone stood with one or two others (all missing) across the entrance.

cites.quote: In 1979, the hole for another similar-sized stone was discovered next to it
Originally standing upright at the entrance to Stonehenge and flanked by additional stones that are now missing

gaps: Petrie 1880 (the source of the numbering, with every stone's state and measurements in 1880) has no free online text that could be found (not on archive.org, Gutenberg, HathiTrust or Wikisource).

Historic England's reports (Abbott & Anderson-Whymark 2012, research report 32/2012) and photo captions (e.g. 'fallen stone 14', stone 23 'collapsed', lintel 127 'temporarily removed' in 1964) are behind a Cloudflare check (HTTP 403) and could not be quoted or checked; Cleal, Walker & Montague 1995 is not online.

No reachable official per-stone condition list: the states of 8, 9, 12, 14, 15, 19, 25, 26, the fallen lintels 120 and 127, and nearly all bluestones are read off Anthony Johnson's numbered plan (Wikimedia Commons, 'as it survives today', 2007) and are marked derived; heights and weights come from The Stones of Stonehenge (a careful personal site, secondary).
Stone 15: the plan shows it fallen, Darvill 2022 counts it missing (17 standing / 7 fallen / 6 missing vs the plan's 17 / 8 / 5).
Station Stone 91 lies fallen (standard descriptions) but no reachable source states it; marked fallen from the absence of a standing height (derived). Its fall direction is unknown.
Leaning bluestones cannot be told from standing ones on the plan; 65 and 67 are uncertain (67 may lean).
No reachable source gives the sarsen circle's inner and outer diameters separately (only ~30 m), nor the bluestone circle and horseshoe diameters (derived from the plan: ~23 m and ~11-13 m).
Exact heights of the middle trilithon pair (53-54, 57-58) overall, and individual lintel sizes, not found.
Fall dates for the circle stones fallen before the 18th century (8, 9, 12, 14, 15, 19, 25, 26) and for 59/160 are unknown; Lockyer's 1620 date for 55/156 is unverified by a modern source.
No modern measured axis azimuth was reachable; Lockyer & Penrose 1901 (49° 34′ 18″) is used.

Which restorations of 1919-20 straightened which stones (e.g. 6, 7 and their lintels) is not documented in a reachable source; the 1958 work re-erected 57, 58, 158 and reset 21, 22, 122; 1959 straightened 60; 1963-64 re-erected 23.
